blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text:
INTRODUCTION TO
TRIGONOMETRY 8

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
There is perhaps nothing which so occupies the
middle position of mathematics as trigonometry.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: - J.F. Herbart (1890)

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already studied about triangles, and in particular, right triangles, in your
earlier classes. Let us take some examples from our surroundings where right triangles
can be imagined to be formed. For instance :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Suppose the students of a school are
visiting Qutub Minar. Now, if a student
is looking at the top of the Minar, a right
triangle can be imagined to be made,
as shown in Fig 8.1. Can the student
find out the height of the Minar, without
actually measuring it?

2. Suppose a girl is sitting on the balcony
of her house located on the bank of a
river. She is looking down at a flower
pot placed on a stair of a temple situated
nearby on the other bank of the river.
A right triangle is imagined to be made
in this situation as shown in Fig.8.2. If
you know the height at which the
person is sitting, can you find the width
of the river?

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.1

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.2

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
3. Suppose a hot air balloon is flying in
the air. A girl happens to spot the
balloon in the sky and runs to her
mother to tell her about it. Her mother
rushes out of the house to look at the
balloon.Now when the girl had spotted
the balloon intially it was at point A.
When both the mother and daughter
came out to see it, it had already
travelled to another point B. Can you
find the altitude of B from the ground?

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In all the situations given above, the distances or heights can be found by using
some mathematical techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called
‘trigonometry’. The word ‘trigonometry’ is derived from the Greek words ‘tri’
(meaning three), ‘gon’ (meaning sides) and ‘metron’ (meaning measure). In fact,
**trigonometry** is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and Babylon. Early
astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets from the Earth.
Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in Engineering and
Physical Sciences are based on trigonometrical concepts.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with
respect to its acute angles, called **trigonometric ratios of the angle**. We will restrict
our discussion to acute angles only. However, these ratios can be extended to other
angles also. We will also define the trigonometric ratios for angles of measure $0^{\circ}$ and
$90^{\circ}$. We will calculate trigonometric ratios for some specific angles and establish
some identities involving these ratios, called **trigonometric identities**.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.2 Trigonometric Ratios

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Section 8.1, you have seen some right triangles
imagined to be formed in different situations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take a right triangle ABC as shown
in Fig. 8.4.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, $\angle$ CAB (or, in brief, angle A) is an
acute angle. Note the position of the side BC
with respect to angle A. It faces $\angle$ A. We call it
the \textit{side opposite} to angle A. AC is the
\textit{hypotenuse} of the right triangle and the side AB
is a part of $\angle$ A. So, we call it the \textit{side}
\textit{adjacent} to angle A.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.4

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that the position of sides change
when you consider angle C in place of A
(see Fig. 8.5).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have studied the concept of ‘ratio’ in
your earlier classes. We now define certain ratios
involving the sides of a right triangle, and call
them trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The trigonometric ratios of the angle A
in right triangle ABC (see Fig. 8.4) are defined
as follows :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{sine of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{cosine of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$tangent \ of \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{BC}{AB}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{cosecant of } \angle A = \frac{1}{\text{sine of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{BC}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$secant \text{ of } \angle A = \frac{1}{\text{cosine of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{AC}{AB}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{cotangent of } \angle A = \frac{1}{\text{tangent of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The ratios defined above are abbreviated as $\sin A$, $\cos A$, $\tan A$, $\text{cosec A}$, $\sec A$
and $\cot A$ respectively. Note that the ratios $\mathbf{cosec A}$, $\mathbf{sec A}$ and $\mathbf{cot A}$ are respectively,
the reciprocals of the ratios $\sin A$, $\cos A$ and $\tan A$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, observe that $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{\frac{BC}{AC}}{\frac{AB}{AC}} = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}$ and $\cot A = \frac{\cos A}{\sin A}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the **trigonometric ratios** of an acute angle in a right triangle express the
relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Why don't you try to define the trigonometric ratios for angle C in the right
triangle? (See Fig. 8.5)

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
The first use of the idea of ‘**sine**’ in the way we use
it today was in the work *Aryabhatiyam* by Aryabhata,
in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word *ardha-jya*
for the half-chord, which was shortened to *jya* or
*jiva* in due course. When the *Aryabhatiyam* was
translated into Arabic, the word *jiva* was retained as
it is. The word *jiva* was translated into *sinus*, which
means curve, when the Arabic version was translated
into Latin. Soon the word *sinus*, also used as *sine*,
became common in mathematical texts throughout
Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund
Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated
notation ‘**sin**’.

The origin of the terms ‘**cosine**’ and ‘**tangent**’ was much later. The cosine function
arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta
called it **kotijya**. The name **cosinus** originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the
English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation ‘**cos**’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Note that the symbol $\sin A$ is used as an
abbreviation for ‘the sine of the angle A’. $\sin A$ is $not$
the product of ‘$\sin$’ and A. ‘$\sin$’ separated from A
has no meaning. Similarly, $\cos A$ is $not$ the product of
‘$\cos$’ and A. Similar interpretations follow for other
trigonometric ratios also.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse
AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle
ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN
perpendicular to AB extended (see Fig. 8.6), how
will the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ PAM differ
from those of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ CAB or from those of $\angle A$ in
$\Delta$ QAN?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To answer this, first look at these triangles. Is $\Delta$ PAM similar to $\Delta$ CAB? From
Chapter 6, recall the AA similarity criterion. Using the criterion, you will see that the
triangles PAM and CAB are similar. Therefore, by the property of similar triangles,
the corresponding sides of the triangles are proportional.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we have $\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AP}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{\text{MP}}{\text{BC}}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: From this, we find $$\frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{AP}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AC}} = \sin \mathrm{A}.$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, $\frac{\mathrm{AM}}{\mathrm{AP}}=\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AC}}=\cos \mathrm{A}, \frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{AM}}=\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\tan \mathrm{A}$ and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This shows that the trigonometric ratios of angle A in $\Delta$ PAM not differ from
those of angle A in $\Delta$ CAB.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the same way, you should check that the value of $\sin A$ (and also of other
trigonometric ratios) remains the same in $\Delta$ QAN also.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric
ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if
the angle remains the same.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** For the sake of convenience, we may write $\sin^2 A$, $\cos^2 A$, etc., in place of
$(\sin A)^2$, $(\cos A)^2$, etc., respectively. But $\csc A = (\sin A)^{-1} \neq \sin^{-1} A$ (it is called sine
inverse $A$). $\sin^{-1} A$ has a different meaning, which will be discussed in higher classes.
Similar conventions hold for the other trigonometric ratios as well. Sometimes, the
Greek letter $\theta$ (theta) is also used to denote an angle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. If we know any one
of the ratios, can we obtain the other ratios? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If in a right triangle ABC, $\sin A = \frac{1}{3}$,
then this means that $\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{1}{3}$, i.e., the
lengths of the sides BC and AC of the triangle
ABC are in the ratio $1:3$ (see Fig. 8.7). So if
BC is equal to $k$, then AC will be $3k$, where
$k$ is any positive number. To determine other
trigonometric ratios for the angle A, we need to find the length of the third side
AB. Do you remember the Pythagoras theorem? Let us use it to determine the
required length AB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\text{AB} = \pm 2\sqrt{2}k$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we get $\text{AB} = 2\sqrt{2}k \quad (\text{Why is AB not } -2\sqrt{2}k ?)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}k}{3k} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Similarly, you can obtain the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of
$\sin A$ or $\cos A$ is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Given $\tan A = \frac{4}{3}$, find the other
trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let us first draw a right $\Delta$ ABC
(see Fig 8.8).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.8

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, we know that $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{4}{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, if BC $= 4k$, then AB $= 3k$, where $k$ is a
positive number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, by using the Pythagoras Theorem, we have

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we can write all the trigonometric ratios using their definitions.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{4k}{5k} = \frac{4}{5}$$
$$\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{3k}{5k} = \frac{3}{5}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\cot A = \frac{1}{\tan A} = \frac{3}{4}$, $\csc A = \frac{1}{\sin A} = \frac{5}{4}$ and $\sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} = \frac{5}{3}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : If $\angle \text{ B}$ and $\angle \text{ Q}$ are
acute angles such that $\sin \text{ B} = \sin \text{ Q}$,
then prove that $\angle \text{ B} = \angle \text{ Q}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let us consider two right
triangles ABC and PQR where
$\sin B = \sin Q$ (see Fig. 8.9).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.9

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have $\sin \mathrm{B} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\sin Q = \frac{PR}{PQ}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}} = \frac{\mathrm{PR}}{\mathrm{PQ}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = k$, say (1)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, using Pythagoras theorem,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{\mathrm{AB}^2 - \mathrm{AC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $QR = \sqrt{PQ^2 - PR^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QR}} = \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{AB}^2 - \mathrm{AC}^2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{k^2\mathrm{PQ}^2 - k^2\mathrm{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}} = \frac{k\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{PQ}^2 - \mathrm{PR}^2}} = k$ \hfill (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: From (1) and (2), we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{PR}} = \frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{PQ}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QR}} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then, by using Theorem 6.4, $\Delta$ ACB $\sim \Delta$ PRQ and therefore, $\angle \mathrm{B} = \angle \mathrm{Q}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Consider $\Delta$ ACB, right-angled at C, in
which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units and $\angle$ ABC = $\theta$
(see Fig. 8.10). Determine the values of
(i) $\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta$,
(ii) $\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta$.
Solution : In $\Delta$ ACB, we have
$$AC = \sqrt{AB^2 - BC^2} = \sqrt{(29)^2 - (21)^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{(29 - 21)(29 + 21)} = \sqrt{(8)(50)} = \sqrt{400} = 20 \text{units}$$
So, $\sin \theta = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{20}{29}$, $\cos \theta = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{21}{29}$.
Now, (i) $\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = \left( \frac{20}{29} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{21}{29} \right)^2 = \frac{20^2 + 21^2}{29^2} = \frac{400 + 441}{841} = 1$,
and (ii) $\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta = \left( \frac{21}{29} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{20}{29} \right)^2 = \frac{(21 + 20)(21 - 20)}{29^2} = \frac{41}{841}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
if $\tan A = 1$, then verify that
$2 \sin A \cos A = 1$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Solution : In $\Delta$ ABC, $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = 1$ (see Fig 8.11)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                                                                              BC = AB

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let AB = BC = $k$, where $k$ is a positive number.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\text{AC} = \sqrt{\text{AB}^2 + \text{BC}^2}$

$= \sqrt{(k)^2 + (k)^2} = k\sqrt{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $2 \sin A \cos A = 2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 1$, which is the required value.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 : In $\Delta$ OPQ, right-angled at P,
OP = 7 cm and OQ – PQ = 1 cm (see Fig. 8.12).
Determine the values of $\sin$ Q and $\cos$ Q.

Solution : In $\Delta$ OPQ, we have

$$OQ^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2$$

i.e., $$(1 + PQ)^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2 \quad \text{(Why?)}$$

i.e., $1 + PQ^2 + 2PQ = OP^2 + PQ^2$

i.e., $1 + 2PQ = 7^2 \quad \text{(Why?)}$

i.e., $PQ = 24 \text{ cm and } OQ = 1 + PQ = 25 \text{ cm}$

So, $\sin Q = \frac{7}{25}$ and $\cos Q = \frac{24}{25}$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.3 Trigonometric Ratios of Some Specific Angles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From geometry, you are already familiar with the construction of angles of $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$,
$60^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. In this section, we will find the values of the trigonometric ratios for these
angles and, of course, for $0^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $45^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is $45^{\circ}$, then
the other angle is also $45^{\circ}$, i.e., $\angle A = \angle C = 45^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.14).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\text{BC} = \text{AB} \quad (\text{Why?})$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, Suppose BC = AB = $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then by Pythagoras Theorem, $\mathrm{AC}^2 = \mathrm{AB}^2 + \mathrm{BC}^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and, therefore, $\text{AC} = a\sqrt{2}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using the definitions of the trigonometric ratios, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\cos 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \tan 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^{\circ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{a} = 1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $\text{cosec } 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 45^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2}$, $\sec 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 45^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2}$, $\cot 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 45^{\circ}} = 1$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now calculate the trigonometric ratios of $30^{\circ}$
and $60^{\circ}$. Consider an equilateral triangle ABC. Since
each angle in an equilateral triangle is $60^{\circ}$, therefore,
$\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = 60^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw the perpendicular AD from A to the side BC
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now $\Delta \mathrm{ABD} \cong \Delta \mathrm{ACD}$ (Why?)
Therefore, $\mathrm{BD}=\mathrm{DC}$
and $\angle \mathrm{BAD}=\angle \mathrm{CAD}$ (CPCT)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now observe that:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\Delta$ ABD is a right triangle, right-angled at D with $\angle$ BAD $= 30^{\circ}$ and $\angle$ ABD $= 60^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: INTRODUCTION TO TRIGONOMETRY

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As you know, for finding the trigonometric ratios, we need to know the lengths of the
sides of the triangle. So, let us suppose that $\text{AB} = 2a$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then, $\text{BD} = \frac{1}{2}\text{BC} = a$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AD = a\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, we have :
$$\sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{2a} = \frac{1}{2}, \cos 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Also, $\quad \operatorname{cosec} 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=2, \quad \sec 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\cos 30^{\circ}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$
$\cot 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\tan 30^{\circ}}=\sqrt{3}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Similarly,
$$\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} , \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2} , \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3} ,$$
$$\text{cosec } 60^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} , \sec 60^{\circ} = 2 \text{ and } \cot 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} .$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of angle
A, if it is made smaller and smaller in the right triangle ABC
(see Fig. 8.16), till it becomes zero. As $\angle$ A gets smaller and
smaller, the length of the side BC decreases.The point C gets
closer to point B, and finally when $\angle$ A becomes very close
to $0^{\circ}$, AC becomes almost the same as AB (see Fig. 8.17).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle A$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, BC gets very close to $0$ and so the value of
$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}$ is very close to $0$. Also, when $\angle A$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, AC is nearly the

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: same as AB and so the value of $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC}$ is very close to 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This helps us to see how we can define the values of $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ when
$A = 0^\circ$. We define : $\mathbf{sin}\ \mathbf{0}^\circ = \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{cos}\ \mathbf{0}^\circ = \mathbf{1}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using these, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\tan 0^{\circ} = \frac{\sin 0^{\circ}}{\cos 0^{\circ}} = 0, \cot 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 0^{\circ}}, \text{ which is not defined. (Why?)}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\sec 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 0^{\circ}} = 1$ and $\csc 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 0^{\circ}}$, which is again not defined.(Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$, when it is made
larger and larger in $\Delta ABC$ till it becomes $90^\circ$. As $\angle A$ gets larger and larger, $\angle C$ gets
smaller and smaller. Therefore, as in the case above, the length of the side AB goes on
decreasing. The point A gets closer to point B. Finally when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$,
$\angle C$ becomes very close to $0^\circ$ and the side AC almost coincides with side BC
(see Fig. 8.18).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle C$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, $\angle A$ is very close to $90^{\circ}$, side AC is nearly the
same as side BC, and so $\sin A$ is very close to $1$. Also when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^{\circ}$,
$\angle C$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, and the side AB is nearly zero, so $\cos A$ is very close to $0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we define : $\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$ and $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, why don’t you find the other trigonometric ratios of $90^\circ$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We shall now give the values of all the trigonometric ratios of $0^{\circ}$, $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$, $60^{\circ}$
and $90^{\circ}$ in Table 8.1, for ready reference.

blocks.label: Table-caption
blocks.text: Table 8.1

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
$\angle A$ $0^\circ$ $30^\circ$ $45^\circ$ $60^\circ$ $90^\circ$
$\sin A$ 0 $\frac{1}{2}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ 1
$\cos A$ 1 $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\frac{1}{2}$ 0
$\tan A$ 0 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1 $\sqrt{3}$ Not defined
cosec A Not defined 2 $\sqrt{2}$ $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1
sec A 1 $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\sqrt{2}$ 2 Not defined
cot A Not defined $\sqrt{3}$ 1 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 0

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Remark :** From the table above you can observe that as $\angle$ A increases from $0^\circ$ to
$90^\circ$, $\sin$ A increases from 0 to 1 and $\cos$ A decreases from 1 to 0.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us illustrate the use of the values in the table above through some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B,
AB = 5 cm and $\angle$ ACB = $30^\circ$ (see Fig. 8.19).
Determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC.
Solution : To find the length of the side BC, we will
choose the trigonometric ratio involving BC and the
given side AB. Since BC is the side adjacent to angle
C and AB is the side opposite to angle C, therefore

$$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}} = \tan \text{C}$$

i.e., $$\frac{5}{\text{BC}} = \tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

which gives $$\text{BC} = 5\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To find the length of the side AC, we consider

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} \qquad (\text{Why?}) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                                                    $AC = 10 \text{ cm}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that alternatively we could have used Pythagoras theorem to determine the third
side in the example above,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $AC = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2} \text{ cm} = 10\text{cm}.$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : In $\Delta$ PQR, right-angled at
Q (see Fig. 8.20), PQ = 3 cm and PR = 6 cm.
Determine $\angle$ QPR and $\angle$ PRQ.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Given $PQ = 3$ cm and $PR = 6$ cm.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{PQ}}{\mathrm{PR}} = \sin \mathrm{R}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\sin R = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\angle PRQ = 30^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and therefore, $\angle QPR = 60^{\circ}$. (Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may note that if one of the sides and any other part (either an acute angle or any
side) of a right triangle is known, the remaining sides and angles of the triangle can be
determined.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 8 : If $\sin (A - B) = \frac{1}{2}$, $\cos (A + B) = \frac{1}{2}$, $0^{\circ} < A + B \leq 90^{\circ}$, $A > B$, find A
and B.

Solution : Since, $\sin (A - B) = \frac{1}{2}$, therefore, $A - B = 30^{\circ}$ (Why?) (1)

Also, since $\cos (A + B) = \frac{1}{2}$, therefore, $A + B = 60^{\circ}$ (Why?) (2)

Solving (1) and (2), we get : $A = 45^{\circ}$ and $B = 15^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solving (1) and (2), we get : $A = 45^{\circ}$ and $B = 15^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.4 Trigonometric Identities

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may recall that an equation is called an identity
when it is true for all values of the variables involved.
Similarly, an equation involving trigonometric ratios
of an angle is called a **trigonometric identity**, if it is
true for all values of the angle(s) involved.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we will prove one trigonometric
identity, and use it further to prove other useful
trigonometric identities.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B (see Fig. 8.21), we have:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Dividing each term of (1) by $AC^2$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\cos^2 \mathbf{A} + \sin^2 \mathbf{A} = 1$ (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This is true for all A such that $0^{\circ} \leq A \leq 90^{\circ}$. So, this is a trigonometric identity.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us now divide (1) by $AB^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $1 + \tan^2 \mathrm{A} = \sec^2 \mathrm{A}$ (3)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Is this equation true for $A = 0^{\circ}$? Yes, it is. What about $A = 90^{\circ}$? Well, $\tan A$ and
sec A are not defined for $A = 90^{\circ}$. So, (3) is true for all A such that $0^{\circ} \le A < 90^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us see what we get on dividing (1) by $\text{BC}^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{AB}{BC}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{BC}{BC}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{AC}{BC}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\cot^2 \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{1} = \operatorname{cosec}^2 \mathbf{A}$ (4)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that cosec A and cot A are not defined for A = $0^\circ$. Therefore (4) is true for
all A such that $0^\circ < \text{A} \le 90^\circ$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Using these identities, we can express each trigonometric ratio in terms of other
trigonometric ratios, i.e., if any one of the ratios is known, we can also determine the
values of other trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see how we can do this using these identities. Suppose we know that


$$\tan A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ . Then, } \cot A = \sqrt{3} \text{ .}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Since, $\sec^2 A = 1 + \tan^2 A = 1 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$, $\sec A = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, and $\cos A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Again, $\sin A = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 A} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{3}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, $\csc A = 2$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 9 : Express the ratios $\cos A$, $\tan A$ and $\sec A$ in terms of $\sin A$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Since $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$, therefore,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 A, \text{ i.e., } \cos A = \pm \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: This gives $\cos A = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Hence, $\tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \frac{\sin A}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}}$ and $\sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 10 : Prove that $\sec A (1 - \sin A)(\sec A + \tan A) = 1$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Solution :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$LHS = \sec A (1 - \sin A)(\sec A + \tan A) = \left( \frac{1}{\cos A} \right) (1 - \sin A) \left( \frac{1}{\cos A} + \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} \right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ = \frac{(1 - \sin A)(1 + \sin A)}{\cos^2 A} = \frac{1 - \sin^2 A}{\cos^2 A} $$

$$ = \frac{\cos^2 A}{\cos^2 A} = 1 = \text{RHS} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 11 : Prove that $\frac{\cot A - \cos A}{\cot A + \cos A} = \frac{\text{cosec A} - 1}{\text{cosec A} + 1}$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : LHS = $\frac{\cot A - \cos A}{\cot A + \cos A} = \frac{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} - \cos A}{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} + \cos A}$
$= \frac{\cos A\left(\frac{1}{\sin A} - 1\right)}{\cos A\left(\frac{1}{\sin A} + 1\right)} = \frac{\left(\frac{1}{\sin A} - 1\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{\sin A} + 1\right)} = \frac{\text{cosec A} - 1}{\text{cosec A} + 1} = \text{RHS}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 : Prove that $\frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}$, using the identity
$\sec^2 \theta = 1 + \tan^2 \theta$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : Since we will apply the identity involving $\sec \theta$ and $\tan \theta$, let us first
convert the LHS (of the identity we need to prove) in terms of $\sec \theta$ and $\tan \theta$ by
dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos \theta$.

$$LHS = \frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{\tan \theta - 1 + \sec \theta}{\tan \theta + 1 - \sec \theta}$$

$$= \frac{(\tan \theta + \sec \theta) - 1}{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta) + 1} = \frac{\{(\tan \theta + \sec \theta) - 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}{\{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta) + 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}$$

$$= \frac{(\tan^2 \theta - \sec^2 \theta) - (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}{\{\tan \theta - \sec \theta + 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}$$

$$= \frac{- 1 - \tan \theta + \sec \theta}{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta + 1) (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{-1}{\tan \theta - \sec \theta} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}, $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the RHS of the identity, we are required to prove.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.5 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
$$ \sin A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \cos A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} $$
$$ \tan A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} . $$
2. $\text{cosec A} = \frac{1}{\sin A} ; \sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} ; \tan A = \frac{1}{\cot A}, \tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} .$
3. If one of the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle is known, the remaining trigonometric
ratios of the angle can be easily determined.
4. The values of trigonometric ratios for angles $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.
5. The value of $\sin A$ or $\cos A$ never exceeds 1, whereas the value of $\sec A$ ($0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ$) or
$\text{cosec A } (0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ)$ is always greater than or equal to 1.
6. $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1,$
$\sec^2 A - \tan^2 A = 1$ for $0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ,$
$\text{cosec}^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 A$ for $0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ.$
